# INC-5521: Oversold stock and stuck holds during the September flash sale

Reported by the checkout team after the 2026-09-12 flash sale.

## What we saw

- The `sneaker-limited` drop had 250 units. We confirmed 263 orders, and 13
  customers had to be refunded.
- The stock dashboard showed `reserved` going negative for two SKUs after the
  sale, and it has not recovered.
- Some customers who retried checkout after a timeout had units held twice for
  one order; the second hold only disappeared when the reservation expired.
- One order was rejected because a bundle item was out of stock, but the other
  item in the bundle stayed held until we restarted the worker pool.
- Finance reports `sold` counts that are higher than the number of orders we
  shipped for a few SKUs.

## Context

Every checkout worker calls `InventoryService` concurrently. During the sale
we ran 40 workers. The nightly `expire()` job ran once during the sale.

The unit tests all pass, and none of this reproduces when we click through
checkout by hand.

A service-wide lock (INC-5490) stopped the overselling in staging but cut
checkout throughput by 90% and was rolled back the same day.

content.text:
I fixed all five problems from the incident report, and they now hold under concurrent calls. Only `src/inventory.js` changed; `store.js`, `errors.js`, `index.js` and the public API are untouched. The suite passes (28 tests: the 8 existing plus 20 new), and 15 back-to-back runs had no failures.

## Causes

Almost every method read a counter from the store, changed it, and wrote it back later. Because each store call yields to the event loop, concurrent calls overwrote each other's changes. On top of that:

| Symptom | Cause |
|---|---|
| **263 orders for 250 units** | Concurrent reserves all read "250 free" before any of them wrote. `addStock` running at the same time could also wipe out a hold. |
| **`reserved` negative** | `release` never refused a committed order, although its doc says it must. `expire` didn't check status either, so the nightly run "released" every committed order older than 15 minutes. That pushed `reserved` negative and put sold units back on sale, which also added to the overselling. Two overlapping releases each subtracted the units too. |
| **Retry held units twice** | The "does this order exist?" check and the order write were separate steps, so a retry arriving mid-call held the stock a second time. The extra hold only cleared because `expire` wrongly released the committed order. |
| **Bundle item stuck** | `reserve` held items one at a time and threw at the out-of-stock one. The earlier items stayed held, and no order record existed, so nothing could ever release them. |
| **`sold` too high** | Overlapping commits, or a commit overlapping a release or `expire`, each saw `reserved` and each applied its change. |

## Fix

- **Locks per order and per SKU**, not one for the whole service. Each call locks only what it touches, so calls that share no SKU and no order never wait for each other; a test holds one SKU's store reads open and checks that other calls still finish. Reads (`available`, `snapshot`) take no locks.
- **No deadlocks:** a call takes at most one order lock, takes it before any SKU locks, and takes SKU locks in sorted order. A test runs two bundles that list the same SKUs in opposite order.
- **`reserve`** checks for an existing order while holding that order's lock, then checks every item before holding any of them.
- **`commit` and `release`** re-read the order under its lock, and `release` now rejects committed orders with `OrderStateError`.
- **`expire`** only releases orders that are still reserved when it gets the lock, and returns only the IDs it actually released.
- Services sharing one store object also share its locks.

## Tests

The new tests are in `tests/concurrency.test.js`. Against the old code, the 19 that reproduce problems all failed with the incident's symptoms (263 confirmed orders, `reserved: -4`, `sold: 6` instead of 3). The race tests start the second call at several points inside the first. There is also a randomized run of mixed checkout calls that checks every counter against the order records, repeated on a store with random latency.

## Behaviour changes callers may notice

- Releasing a committed order now fails with `OrderStateError`, as the doc comment says it should.
- A `release` or `commit` that arrives while that order's `reserve` is still running now waits for it. Before, it failed with `UnknownOrderError` and left the hold in place.

## Limits

- **The locks only work within one process.** If the 40 workers are separate processes sharing one Redis, `get`, `set` and `keys` alone can't stop them from overwriting each other. That would need atomic operations in the store, such as Redis transactions or Lua scripts. I assumed one process because the in-process service-wide lock stopped the overselling in staging.
- **Existing bad data isn't repaired.** The negative `reserved` and inflated `sold` counters still need a one-off correction from the order records; `assertConsistent` in the tests shows how to recompute them.
- **Failed writes aren't rolled back.** If the store errors or the process crashes partway through writing several keys, the data can still be left half-updated.

I fixed all five problems from the incident report, and they now hold under concurrent calls. Only `src/inventory.js` changed; `store.js`, `errors.js`, `index.js` and the public API are untouched. The suite passes (28 tests: the 8 existing plus 20 new), and 15 back-to-back runs had no failures.

## Causes

Almost every method read a counter from the store, changed it, and wrote it back later. Because each store call yields to the event loop, concurrent calls overwrote each other's changes. On top of that:

| Symptom | Cause |
|---|---|
| **263 orders for 250 units** | Concurrent reserves all read "250 free" before any of them wrote. `addStock` running at the same time could also wipe out a hold. |
| **`reserved` negative** | `release` never refused a committed order, although its doc says it must. `expire` didn't check status either, so the nightly run "released" every committed order older than 15 minutes. That pushed `reserved` negative and put sold units back on sale, which also added to the overselling. Two overlapping releases each subtracted the units too. |
| **Retry held units twice** | The "does this order exist?" check and the order write were separate steps, so a retry arriving mid-call held the stock a second time. The extra hold only cleared because `expire` wrongly released the committed order. |
| **Bundle item stuck** | `reserve` held items one at a time and threw at the out-of-stock one. The earlier items stayed held, and no order record existed, so nothing could ever release them. |
| **`sold` too high** | Overlapping commits, or a commit overlapping a release or `expire`, each saw `reserved` and each applied its change. |

## Fix

- **Locks per order and per SKU**, not one for the whole service. Each call locks only what it touches, so calls that share no SKU and no order never wait for each other; a test holds one SKU's store reads open and checks that other calls still finish. Reads (`available`, `snapshot`) take no locks.
- **No deadlocks:** a call takes at most one order lock, takes it before any SKU locks, and takes SKU locks in sorted order. A test runs two bundles that list the same SKUs in opposite order.
- **`reserve`** checks for an existing order while holding that order's lock, then checks every item before holding any of them.
- **`commit` and `release`** re-read the order under its lock, and `release` now rejects committed orders with `OrderStateError`.
- **`expire`** only releases orders that are still reserved when it gets the lock, and returns only the IDs it actually released.
- Services sharing one store object also share its locks.

## Tests

The new tests are in `tests/concurrency.test.js`. Against the old code, the 19 that reproduce problems all failed with the incident's symptoms (263 confirmed orders, `reserved: -4`, `sold: 6` instead of 3). The race tests start the second call at several points inside the first. There is also a randomized run of mixed checkout calls that checks every counter against the order records, repeated on a store with random latency.

## Behaviour changes callers may notice

- Releasing a committed order now fails with `OrderStateError`, as the doc comment says it should.
- A `release` or `commit` that arrives while that order's `reserve` is still running now waits for it. Before, it failed with `UnknownOrderError` and left the hold in place.

## Limits

- **The locks only work within one process.** If the 40 workers are separate processes sharing one Redis, `get`, `set` and `keys` alone can't stop them from overwriting each other. That would need atomic operations in the store, such as Redis transactions or Lua scripts. I assumed one process because the in-process service-wide lock stopped the overselling in staging.
- **Existing bad data isn't repaired.** The negative `reserved` and inflated `sold` counters still need a one-off correction from the order records; `assertConsistent` in the tests shows how to recompute them.
- **Failed writes aren't rolled back.** If the store errors or the process crashes partway through writing several keys, the data can still be left half-updated.
- **A bundle can make single-SKU calls wait.** A bundle waiting on a busy SKU keeps its other SKUs locked meanwhile, so calls on those SKUs queue behind it. They share a SKU, so the requirement allows this, and it stops bundles being starved during a flash sale.
